opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is an example people often attribute to Ilya Sutskever, and I think it captures something really important about why next-token prediction is a much richer objective than it sounds.

Think about what's actually happening at the end of a detective novel. You've got hundreds of pages of setup: characters with alibis, motives, little throwaway details about who was in the library at nine o'clock, a muddy boot print, someone who conveniently lied about where they were. Then you reach the line, "And the murderer is..." The next word is a name. If you're just doing shallow pattern matching, like "which character name appeared most often," or "which name tends to follow this phrase," you're going to get it wrong most of the time. Good mystery writers deliberately make the obvious suspect *not* the answer.

So to get that one token right reliably, the model has to have done something that looks a lot like reasoning over a representation of the story. It needs to track entities: who these people are, how they relate to each other. It needs some notion of time and causality: what happened before what, who could physically have been where. It needs to model beliefs and deception: this character *said* X, but the narrator hinted that was false. And it has to integrate all of that into a coherent picture of the fictional world, and then ask which explanation is consistent with everything.

That's basically what we mean by a world model: an internal structure that represents the state of some situation and lets you make predictions about it, rather than just memorizing surface statistics.

Now, I want to be a bit careful here, because it's a thought experiment, not proof that today's models actually do this. The claim is more that the *objective* pushes in that direction. If you want to minimize prediction loss on text written by humans about a world, the best possible strategy eventually involves modeling the world and the minds producing the text. Whether a given model has actually learned that, or is getting by with a pile of clever heuristics, is an empirical question. And that's exactly where interpretability comes in: we can open the model up and check whether there are internal representations that track things like entity states, relationships, or causal structure, and whether the model actually *uses* them when it makes predictions.

So for me the murder mystery is a nice intuition pump. It shows why "just predicting the next word" isn't trivial, and it motivates looking inside these systems to see what kind of understanding, if any, they've built to do it.

r001.rationale: The response says the model must track who the characters are and how they relate, including deception, to infer the murderer’s name at the reveal.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the murder mystery example is one I like because it makes the abstract point really concrete. Think about what it takes to predict the next word when the detective gathers everyone in the drawing room and says, "The murderer is..." If you're just doing surface-level statistics, matching on the last few sentences, you have basically no chance. The name that comes next isn't determined by local patterns. It's determined by everything that happened across the whole book: who had the key, who lied about where they were on Tuesday night, which alibi quietly fell apart in chapter twelve.

So to get that one token right, the model has to have been tracking state the entire time. It needs some representation of the characters, their motives, their locations, what each of them knows, which clues are red herrings and which are real. And then it has to do something like inference over that representation to figure out who's actually consistent with all the evidence. That's a world model. Maybe not in the full sense a cognitive scientist would mean, but it's an internal structure that mirrors the causal and logical structure of the story, not just the text.

And the thing I find compelling about framing it this way is that it falls directly out of the training objective. Nobody told the model "please build a world model." It's just that next-token prediction, pushed hard enough on data that was generated by humans who have world models, forces you toward the same thing. The loss on that one token at the reveal is a lot lower if you've been doing the detective work all along. The mystery novel is kind of the extreme case, but I'd argue it's happening in a softer way everywhere. Predicting the next word in a physics textbook or a recipe or a legal contract rewards having some structured representation of what's being described.

Now, where it gets interesting for people doing interpretability, which is my area, is that this is a claim you can actually go test. If the model is tracking who the murderer is, there should be something in the activations that corresponds to that, and you should be able to find it and manipulate it. And a lot of recent work suggests that's roughly what we see, at least for simpler cases like board games or spatial layouts. Whether the representations are as clean and as general as we'd like is still very much an open question, but the basic picture, that prediction demands modeling, I think holds up pretty well.

r001.rationale: The response says the model should represent characters, motives, locations, knowledge, and clues, but it does not clearly identify how people interact with one another as something it must represent.

astra-6.text:
Think about what happens when a detective says, “And the murderer is…” Predicting the next name requires more than knowing which words commonly follow that phrase. You need to track the story: who was where, who had a motive, who had access to the weapon, and whose alibi contradicts the evidence.

An internal world model is a representation of those underlying facts and relationships. It lets the model connect clues that might be scattered across many pages and infer which character fits them. The next word is just a name, but predicting it well can require reasoning about the whole situation.

That doesn’t mean every next-word prediction requires a world model, or that a model has to represent the story exactly as a human would. But if you want to predict well across unfamiliar mysteries, rather than just guess from familiar plot patterns, it helps to represent what’s happening behind the words.

r001.rationale: The response says the model should track characters’ locations, motives, access, and alibis, but it does not clearly identify how people interact with one another as something the model must represent.

sol-6.1.text:
Because the next word can depend on everything that happened earlier in the story. If the detective says, “The murderer is…” then predicting the name means keeping track of who had a motive, who had access to the weapon, whose alibi holds up, and who knows what.

The idea is that a good model can’t rely only on which words tend to appear next to each other. It benefits from an internal representation of the situation—the characters, their actions, and the causal relationships between events. That’s what I mean by a world model here. It doesn’t have to be a perfect simulation, but it needs to capture enough of the story’s underlying structure to make the reveal make sense.

r001.rationale: The response says the model should track characters, their actions, motives, access, and causal relationships between events, but it does not clearly identify how people interact with one another as something it must represent.
